name: Earthjustice: climate and clean energy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of greenhouse gas kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population; the small US coal-smoke share is left in the world figure.
summary: Earthjustice (San Francisco), the largest US non-profit environmental law firm, litigates and advocates on climate and clean energy, healthy communities and biodiversity; this model is its climate and clean-energy work (our judgment: 45% of programme spending, $61.8M of the $137.4M it spent itself in the year to June 2025, after $16.8M of donated legal work and advertising). It counts three wins of fiscal 2022-2025 we can put tonnes on: EPA's 2023 oil and gas methane rule and 2024 power-plant carbon standards (at the same tonnes, status and credit steps as Clean Air Task Force's model) and the US coal plants that closed in 2022-2025, of which advocacy is credited with 15% and Earthjustice with a tenth of that, plus 50% for its many state and other wins. At the defaults a dollar given averts about 0.0057 tonnes of CO₂e (about $175 a tonne), 0.0025 years of healthy life per $1,000, about half from the methane rule and half from the coal closings; it is low because each win is shared with many groups and with what utilities and governments would have done anyway, and the federal rules have since been weakened or repealed. The biggest uncertainties are the years a won reform counts, the discount rate and Earthjustice's share of each win; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no tonne is measured for its work.

rows.label: US coal-fired capacity retired, 2022-2025
Electricity a retiring gigawatt of coal made in a year before it closed
rows.explainer: A gigawatt running all year makes 8.76 TWh; US coal plants ran at roughly 40% of capacity in the 2020s, and the plants that retire are the older, less-used ones. Our judgment, a capacity factor of about 35% (20% to 50%): 3.0 TWh (1.75 to 4.4).

rows.explainer: EIA's 2.31 pounds per kWh for coal in 2023, in tonnes per MWh (× 0.4536 kg per pound): 1.048. The range: the fleet average, while the old plants that retire burn a little more coal per MWh (up to 1.15).

rows.label: CO₂ per MWh of the power that replaces it
rows.explainer: Retired coal is replaced by gas (0.96 pounds per kWh in 2023, 0.435 t per MWh: EIA, same table), wind, solar, storage and lower demand. Our judgment, 0.25 t per MWh (0.1 to 0.45, the top all gas).

rows.label: Share of each EPA rule due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won policy that is the advocates' doing rather than what governments and events would have done anyway. Both EPA rules take it, as in Clean Air Task Force's model; Earthjustice's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row. The rules are in, so this is not a chance of winning.

rows.label: Coal retirements: share due to advocacy and litigation at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: Most US coal retirements of 2022-2025 were economic (cheap gas and renewables, ageing plants), with federal rules (coal ash, effluent, haze) and state clean-energy laws behind others. Advocacy before utility commissions and in court (Sierra Club's Beyond Coal campaign, Earthjustice, state groups) set dates and blocked life extensions. Our judgment, 15% (5% to 35%), below the shared 30% for a won climate policy because a retirement is mostly a utility's economic choice.

Evidence adjustment: how far the regulators' estimates and our coal arithmetic should be trusted
rows.explainer: EPA's tonnes are ex-ante estimates, sometimes too high (compliance short of the rule) and sometimes too low (leaks larger than inventories say); the coal tonnes rest on judged output and replacement. Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), as in Clean Air Task Force's model for the same rules; delivery and repeal are in each branch's implementation row.

rows.label: EPA methane rule: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: EPA's baseline already holds state rules; some operators would have cut leaks anyway. Our judgment, 80% (60% to 100%), the same as Clean Air Task Force's model for the same rule (one figure for one rule).

rows.label: EPA methane rule: Earthjustice's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Earthjustice represented health and environmental groups in EPA's rulemaking and in defending the rule in the D.C. Circuit, beside the Environmental Defense Fund (which led the field), NRDC, Clean Air Task Force, Sierra Club and state groups. Our judgment, 8% (3% to 20%), a little below Clean Air Task Force's 10% (its methane work is a specialism; Earthjustice's was one of many dockets), so the named groups' shares leave most of the credit to the Environmental Defense Fund and the rest.

rows.label: EPA methane rule: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Since 2025 EPA has pushed most compliance dates to 2027, loosened flare and vent rules and proposed rescinding the super-emitter programme; the rule still stands and is defended in court (Earthjustice among the defenders). Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%), the same as Clean Air Task Force's model.

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: EPA's baseline already holds announced retirements and the Inflation Reduction Act; some further cuts would have come anyway. Our judgment, 80% (50% to 100%), the same as Clean Air Task Force's model.

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: Earthjustice's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Earthjustice represented public-health and environmental groups through the power-plant carbon rules from West Virginia v. EPA (2022) to the 2024 standards and their defence, beside NRDC, Sierra Club, the Environmental Defense Fund, Clean Air Task Force and states. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%), the same as Clean Air Task Force's share: similar roles, and together a fifth of the advocacy, leaving most of it to the others.

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: EPA repealed the existing-coal guidelines and the carbon-capture standards in 2026 after rescinding the 2009 endangerment finding; what remains is the chance courts or a later administration restore them within the years counted. Our judgment, 5% (1% to 20%), the same as Clean Air Task Force's model.

rows.label: Coal retirements: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: what would have happened anyway is counted once, in the advocacy share (the economics and rules behind most closings) and in the years a closing counts (it would have come some years later); counting it here too would count it twice (templates.md Convention 5).

rows.label: Coal retirements: Earthjustice's share of the advocacy resources behind them

source.title: Earthjustice, Annual Report, fiscal year 2025

rows.explainer: Earthjustice argues coal-retirement and replacement cases before utility commissions (the annual report lists progress in 2024-25 in Colorado, Kentucky, Michigan, Montana and West Virginia, and more than 130 matters in 18 states beyond New York and California in a year), often as counsel to Sierra Club, whose Beyond Coal campaign, funded by Bloomberg Philanthropies, is the field's largest. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%) of the advocacy behind the period's closings.

rows.label: Coal retirements: share of the counted closings that stay closed

Campbell among them, which Earthjustice is contesting), and a few retired units may be repowered. Our judgment, 85% (60% to 100%).

rows.label: Other climate wins of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value

source.title: Earthjustice, Annual Report, fiscal year 2025
source.quote: We have won 100 percent of these offshore drilling cases

rows.explainer: The three branches are the period's largest countable climate wins, but much of the work isn't in them: the defence of EPA's 2024 vehicle standards and California's clean-car rules (since rescinded or overturned by Congress), gas plants blocked (Newburgh, New York) and other state wins (all-electric buildings in New York, neighbourhood electrification in California, efficiency and solar programmes: over $150M of incentives in Colorado alone), New York City's congestion pricing, offshore and onshore oil and gas lease sales challenged (nine of nine offshore cases won since 2018), and coal and gas cases abroad. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 50% of the modelled value (20% to 100%), above Clean Air Task Force's 30% because more of Earthjustice's climate work is state cases too small to model one by one.

rows.label: Side effect: smog-forming pollution cut by the methane rule, as a share of its branch's value

source.title: US EPA (2023), Regulatory Impact Analysis for the final oil and natural gas standards
source.note: About 56 (2028) to 74 (2038) ozone deaths a year avoided from the rule's VOC cuts.

rows.explainer: EPA's methane rule also cuts volatile organic compounds near wells, about 56 to 74 local ozone deaths a year (EPA's tables). Valued at the shared rates that is about an eighth of the methane tonnes' heat-death value, and heat is about half of a methane tonne's value in the shared conversion (the other half methane's own ozone): 6% (3% to 12%) of the methane branch, the same deaths Clean Air Task Force's model counts as 1% of its larger, mostly European total.

rows.explainer: The branches' own combined adjustments apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: The methane rule's share of the expected tonnes, weighted by tonnes a year before waits and years counted (which can't feed a conversion row). The shared climate conversion values this share by methane's own, earlier warming and the ozone it forms (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: The power-plant standards and the coal closings cut coal burnt in US power plants; the methane rule's tonnes are leaks, not burning (its local smog is the side effect above).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of these fuel tonnes, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Both fuel branches cut US coal-plant tonnes: the shared figure for them (facts: climate.us_coal_power_smoke_factor, 0.067 of the world average). The gas that replaces part of the coal smokes far less and is already netted out of the tonnes.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: Deaths a source counts directly beside the tonnes: none here. Coal smoke is in the air-pollution weight; methane's ozone and earlier warming are in the shared conversion through the methane share.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per year of the period
rows.formula: (usmeth_downstream * usmeth_total_adj + pwr_downstream * pwr_total_adj + coal_downstream * coal_total_adj) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + usmeth_downstream * usmeth_total_adj * voc_health_share / period_years
rows.explainer: Each win's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed and spread over the period's four years, with the other wins added as a share, and the methane rule's smog cut as a share of its branch.
